subject: using negative_infinity() or positive_infinity() as lower and upper bounds in a truncated distribution

messages.author: 33d5534e21fbbe0f
messages.subject: using negative_infinity() or positive_infinity() as lower and upper bounds in a truncated distribution
parts:
Hi, In order to avoid conditional statements on the setting of truncation points, I need to use negative_infiniity() as a lower bound for a truncated prior on an element of a parameter matrix?  Is this okay to do?

Thank you.

--
Thank you, Terrance Savitsky

messages.author: 33d5534e21fbbe0f
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] using negative_infinity() or positive_infinity() as lower and upper bounds in a truncated distribution
parts:
Bob,  I'd appreciate your help to think through a problem.   what i want to do is set truncation limits for t[i,d] based on y[i,d].   if y[i] = 1, then t[i,d] < gamma[d,1]  (where gamma is an array of ordered vectors).   if y[i,d] = number_of_categories, then t[i,d] > gamma[d,number_of_categories - 1]; otherwise gamma[d,y[i,d] - 1] <  t[i,d] <= gamma[d,y[i,d]].   the easiest way to impose the truncation boundaries without employing conditional statements is to just place -infinity and +infinity on the left and right ends of the gamma[d].   Of course, since I set the scale of t[i,d] (to identify the model) I may readily choose a value for abs(infinity) that will work - such as 1e3, for example, and that should work fine.  I just wanted to so something less hack-ish.   I suspected negative_infinity() / positive_infinity() wouldn't work unless the truncation recognized and turned off the boundary.   

If I don't want to use this hack approach, I could try directly augmenting lp__ using if_else(), but I don't think it's flexible enough - since there are 3 possible outcomes that determine the update, not 2, and if_else() doesn't look like it is designed to chain or nest multiple if_else() checks.

Thanks, Terrance.

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] using negative_infinity() or positive_infinity() as lower and upper bounds in a truncated distribution
parts:
On 9/21/12 1:53 PM, terrance savitsky wrote:
> Bob, I'd appreciate your help to think through a problem. what i want to do is set truncation limits for t[i,d] based
> on y[i,d]. if y[i] = 1, then t[i,d] < gamma[d,1] (where gamma is an array of ordered vectors). if y[i,d] =
> number_of_categories, then t[i,d] > gamma[d,number_of_categories - 1]; otherwise gamma[d,y[i,d] - 1] < t[i,d] <=
> gamma[d,y[i,d]].

My head hurts just thinking about this.

There's no way to conditionally declare a variable
as having a lower bound, upper bound, or both.

> the easiest way to impose the truncation boundaries without employing conditional statements is to
> just place -infinity and +infinity on the left and right ends of the gamma[d]. Of course, since I set the scale of
> t[i,d] (to identify the model) I may readily choose a value for abs(infinity) that will work - such as 1e3, for example,
> and that should work fine. I just wanted to so something less hack-ish. I suspected negative_infinity() /
> positive_infinity() wouldn't work unless the truncation recognized and turned off the boundary.

Right -- it won't work yet.

And it's a bit of a pain to add because
of the way integer vs. floating-point arithmetic
works and the way auto-dif works (not too bad, but
hours we don't have). We'll add it soon as it's
the right limit behavior.

> If I don't want to use this hack approach, I could try directly augmenting lp__ using if_else(), but I don't think it's
> flexible enough - since there are 3 possible outcomes that determine the update, not 2, and if_else() doesn't look like
> it is designed to chain or nest multiple if_else() checks.

if_else() will certainly chain, but it's inefficient
in that it always evaluates both branches (unlike
C++'s ternary operator or a true branch). You can
also use Marcus's hack I mentioned a day or two ago and
use

int<lower=0,upper=1> bool_value;

bool_value <- ...
for (dummy in 1:bool_value)
body;

The body only gets evaluated if bool_value = 1.

We'll add conditionals as soon as we get the lower-level
bugs sorted out.

- Bob

messages.author: cab04b8f0759c712
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] using negative_infinity() or positive_infinity() as lower and upper bounds in a truncated distribution
parts:
Terrance,

One thing that could be done is to separate your y variable into a y
with a lower bound, a y with an upper bound, and a y that is bounded
both below and above. I'm thinking along the lines of how we suggest
splitting observed data and missing data (covered in the manual).

If the bounds are fixed for each of those subsets, I think it should
work. The preprocessing can be done in R or perhaps a transformed data
block, as long as the bounds are conditional on data.


Daniel

messages.author: 33d5534e21fbbe0f
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] using negative_infinity() or positive_infinity() as lower and upper bounds in a truncated distribution
parts: Thanks Bob and Daniel for your help.   Your approaches would work fine.  I would input bool_1, bool_2, bool_3 as data and then use the loop constructions Bob lays to ensure only the correct statements are executed.  Marcus had earlier provided me a workaround for declaring different restriction limits on a vector (or matrix) of parameters.   His workaround involves generating a same-sized vector of real<lower=0,upper=1> parameters and using lower and upper bounds generated as a function of a vector of (parameter) cutpoints and the data (as you suggested Daniel) to generate a transformed parameter vector.   The workaround anyway will require that i use -infinity and infinity for some of the lower an upper bounds in the parameter vector.   So I'm going to anyway have to employ the hack of creating a transformed data constant set to a large value to simulate infinity.   If I have to anyway do this, then I already have a workaround setting truncation limits in the assignment of the distribution that just involve augmenting a vector of cutpoints that involve placing +/- infinity on each end, respectively.  Then no conditional statements are required.   I was trying to avoid the hack of having to fix a large value for infinity, but it is unavoidable.
